# Error-detecting and error-correcting codes (`error_correcting_codes`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by binary_numbers, information_theory, combinatorics_permutations, logic_gates_switching
- Core idea: Add extra digits calculated from the message so that mistakes show up and can be repaired without asking again. One parity digit, chosen so that the number of ones in a group is even, reveals any single wrong digit but not where it is. Hamming's code locates it: to four data digits add three parity digits, each checking a different overlapping group of positions (1,3,5,7; 2,3,6,7; 4,5,6,7). The pattern of failed checks, read as a binary number, is the position of the wrong digit, which is then simply inverted. In general, if any two valid code words differ in at least d places, the code detects d-1 errors or corrects up to half of that, rounded down.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sending everything three times and taking a majority; it works but triples the cost where a good code adds a small fraction
  - Expecting a code to cope with more errors than it was designed for; it then 'corrects' to a wrong word without warning
  - Forgetting that errors often come in bursts, which need interleaving or codes designed for bursts
  - Confusing these codes with secret codes; they add redundancy for reliability and hide nothing
- History: americas: 1940s – parity checks in Bell Labs relay computers stop the machine on an error; 1947–1948 Hamming devises single-error-correcting codes at Bell Labs, cited by Shannon in 1948 and published in 1950 after patent delays; 1949 Golay's codes; 1954 Reed–Muller codes; 1960 Reed–Solomon codes; 1962 Gallager's low-density parity-check codes; 1967 Viterbi's decoding algorithm; europe: 1993 – turbo codes (Berrou, Glavieux and Thitimajshima, presented at Geneva) come close to Shannon's limit
- Read:
  - Richard W. Hamming, Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes, Bell System Technical Journal 29 (1950)
  - Thomas M. Thompson, From Error-Correcting Codes through Sphere Packings to Simple Groups (1983)
